**Second Person**

My brother wanted the house emptied by Friday. He'd rented the dumpster on Monday, and by Wednesday the things our mother had spent sixty years gathering were leaving through the front door in black bags. He was not heartless. He was practical, which can look identical from a distance, and grief had made him more practical still, as though the mess of her possessions were an insult to the clean fact of her death.

I was on a stepstool wiping out the cabinet above the refrigerator when I found the box. Tin, once blue, rusted at the corners. I knew it before I touched it. It had lived up there my whole childhood, brought down only for ceremony—cardamom bread at Christmas, the lamb cake at Easter with its fleece of coconut.

"Taking that?" he asked, not looking up from the shelf he was dismantling.

"It's just recipes," I said. He shrugged. That was the entire negotiation for the heaviest thing I carried out of the house.

That night I opened it at my own kitchen table, and it was not just recipes.

Two hundred cards, maybe more. Most in her hand—that quick cursive leaning like something blown sideways. Some in my grandmother's blunt pencil. A few in a looping script I couldn't place, women dead longer than I'd been alive, passing a pie crust down through the tin like a rumor. The printed dividers said BREADS, DESSERTS, MAIN DISHES, but she had added her own tabs in ballpoint: COMPANY. SICK. FOR BAD DAYS.

Under FOR BAD DAYS, a dark chocolate cake with one layer, titled in 1974: *Divorce Cake*. On the back—*Made this the day it was final. Ate half of it standing at the counter. Do not judge me.*

Under SICK, a rice pudding. On the back, in different ink, added years later: *for fevers. For heartbreak. For Tuesdays.*

I sat with the box for three hours. My tea went cold twice. It was like reading a diary that happened to be organized by course. Here was her handwriting young and careful, then quick, then shaky at the end. Here was a lemon square with the note: *Margie asked for this at every visit for thirty years and I always said no. She can have it now.* I never knew who Margie was. My mother had a Margie—a whole person, a thirty-year campaign of withheld lemon squares—and I never knew.

And then, filed in DESSERTS between the lemon squares and the shortbread, in fat pencil letters: *PANCAKS. 1. pour. 2. wate. 3. flip wen bubuls.* Mine. I was seven. She kept it for forty years among the recipes that mattered, as though a child's pancakes were part of the canon.

I don't have children. My brother's kids are grown and far away. There is no one to leave this box to, and I sat there understanding that she probably knew that, and kept the cards anyway, and that maybe keeping things no one will inherit is its own kind of hope, or its own kind of letter.

Because here is what I noticed, around midnight, holding a card for beef stew that still smelled faintly of bay leaves: every recipe is written in the second person. All of them. Cream the butter. Fold in the eggs gently—don't stir; you'll knock the air out. Let it rest. You'll know it's done when you can smell it from the other room. She never used a timer, my mother. She used the house. She used her nose standing in the doorway in her slippers. And every instruction on every card was addressed to a *you* she could not see and did not name—someone in a kitchen she would never stand in, still alive because she once was.

The dead can't tell us anything, we say. But they can instruct us. Instruction is what they have. Turn the dough once. Don't open the oven door. Don't worry if it cracks.

That last one was on the back of the cheesecake card, in her late, shaking hand, underlined twice: *Don't worry if it cracks. It's going to crack.*

I made the cardamom bread at one in the morning because I could not not make it. I didn't have enough cardamom, so I substituted, as her own cards taught me: cinnamon and a little black pepper, nobody's grandmother will know. I creamed the butter. I kneaded it the number of times she specified, which was not minutes but turns—*forty turns, then stop, you're not mad at it*. The house began to smell like every December of my life arriving at once, and I stood in the doorway in my slippers like a woman checking her own nose, and I understood her completely for the first time in thirty years and thirty seconds.

The loaf cracked down the middle. It's going to crack.

It didn't taste like hers. It tasted like mine—near hers, the way my face in certain mirrors is near hers, mine and hers at once. I ate it warm at the counter, standing up, which I believe is correct, and which she would have judged me gently for, and then joined.

At the very back of the tin, under a rubber band, was a fresh pack of blank cards. She'd bought them and never got to them. There was always more time; that's the belief you live inside; that's the whole trick of being alive.

So I took one out and started a card. Cardamom bread, with my corrections, my substitutions, the turns counted my way. And when I got to the part where it goes in the pan, I wrote what she would have written, what all of us are always writing, forward into kitchens we will never see, to a *you* I can't imagine yet:

*You'll know it's ready when the house smells like someone is coming home.*

The prompt is beautifully open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation for creative freedom. Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting, moving, or thoughtful to write.

I could write:
1. A short story
2. An essay/meditation on something
3. Something experimental/meta about the prompt itself
4. A poem (though 1000 words of poetry is a lot)
5. A personal-feeling narrative
6. Something philosophical

The meta-approach (writing about the blank page, about having 1000 words) is tempting but a bit overdone. Let me think about what would actually be compelling.

What comes to me? Let me brainstorm genuinely:

- A story about a lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the previous keeper
- A meditation on time, mortality, attention
- A story about someone who repairs things—clocks, maybe—and what that means
- Something about the ocean, about depth
- A story told in second person
- Something about memory and its unreliability
- A piece about a specific moment—a woman on a train, a man at a funeral
- Something about language itself, words as physical objects

Actually, what comes to me is this: the phrase "whatever comes to you" — the idea of things coming to us, unbidden. Thoughts, memories, grief, love. What comes to us versus what we go seeking.

Let me try writing a piece that starts concrete and becomes something larger. Maybe a story about a specific person in a specific moment that opens outward.

Idea: A woman inherits her mother's recipe box, and the recipes aren't just recipes—they're records of a life. The stains, the annotations. "Halve this—Dad doesn't need a whole pie." That could be moving. Food writing, memory, grief.

Or: A man who works the night shift at a 24-hour diner and the regulars who come in. That's a bit well-worn.

Or: Something about the moon. Or about a specific hour of the day—the 4pm light.

Or I could write something strange and lovely—a piece about a town where everyone's words are visible, or where silence is collected.

Let me try the recipe box idea but make it feel fresh. Or actually—let me think about what's most alive right now as I imagine writing it.

Actually here's another idea: a piece about the last speaker of a language, or about a word that doesn't exist in English but should. Or a letter. Letters are intimate and immediate.

What about a piece structured around an inventory? "Things my father left behind" — a list that becomes a story. That form (list as narrative) can be powerful. Each object carries a memory.

Or a story about the space between two people—say, siblings cleaning out their childhood home. The house as archive.

Let me draft the recipe box / inherited kitchen idea:

---

Opening: "The recipe box was the last thing I took from the house, and I took it because no one else wanted it."

Then the discovery: cards in her mother's handwriting, but also in her grandmother's, and a few in handwriting she doesn't recognize. Annotations. The recipe box as palimpsest.

Details: "Halve the salt—your father's heart." "Made for Danny's graduation. He cried." "Do not make this when sad; it will not save you. Made it anyway."

The story emerges: the mother's life, a relationship between mother and daughter (the narrator), maybe an unresolved thing—the narrator and her mother didn't speak for some period, or the mother had a hidden life, or simply the ordinary estrangement of adulthood that can never now be repaired because the mother is dead.

The turn: the narrator finds a recipe in her own childhood handwriting—"pancakes, age 7" with misspellings—and realizes her mother kept it for forty years. Or the narrator finds a recipe for something the mother made the night something happened.

Ending: the narrator makes one of the recipes. The act of cooking as communion with the dead. The taste as memory. Maybe the last card is blank, and the narrator writes on it—beginning her own recipe, her own record. That's a good ending image: the blank card, the pen.

Let me think about length: 1000 words. That's a full short piece. I should pace it—maybe 150-200 words for setup, the middle section exploring the cards, the discovery/revelation, and the ending.

Actually, I want to make sure the piece has specificity that makes it feel real, not generic sentimental. Specific dishes: cardamom bread, a beef stew, "Divorce Cake" (dark humor—she made it the day the divorce was final). That's a good detail—a card titled something wry.

Details to include:
- The physical box: tin, rusted at the corners, or wooden, paint flaking. Hinge that squeaks.
- Dividers with handwritten tabs or the original printed tabs (Breads, Desserts, Main Dishes) with a few odd ones added: "For Bad Days," "Company," "Sick."
- "Sick" as a tab—recipes for when someone is sick. That's tender.
- Cards written by different people—mother, grandmother, an aunt, one in unfamiliar male handwriting (the father's? He cooked once a year?).
- Annotations that tell a story: "too sweet," "Margie asked for this at every visit and I never gave it to her. She can have it now." (implying Margie died)
- A recipe card that isn't a recipe: measurements for wallpaper paste, or a phone number, or a list ("Things to do when he's gone: ..."). Hmm, that might be too dramatic. Maybe something quieter—on the back of a card, in pencil: "She liked this one." The narrator doesn't know who "she" was.

The emotional core: recipes are instructions for the future written in the past. Every recipe is a letter to whoever cooks it next. "Cream the butter and sugar until it looks right." "You'll know it's done when you can smell it from the other room." The mother teaching through the card, across death. The word "you" in every recipe—the mother saying "you" to the daughter without knowing she was saying it.

That's the philosophical heart I can articulate: A recipe is written in the second person. It's all imperative address: "Stir until... Fold in... Let rest." The dead woman speaking in commands and assurances. "Don't worry if it cracks." That could be the line that lands—because it means both the cake and everything else.

Ending options:
1. The narrator cooks something. The taste is almost right. "Almost" is the point.
2. The narrator finds the blank cards at the back and begins writing her own.
3. The narrator reads a card aloud in the empty kitchen—the imperative voice filling the room.

Maybe combine: she cooks her mother's cardamom bread (or the stew), following the instructions, and at some instruction—"Don't worry if it cracks"—she hears her mother's voice, not as ghost-magic but as memory made audible by the imperative mood. Then she writes the first card of her own, in the same second person, addressed forward. "For whoever comes next."

The theme connects to the prompt! "Write whatever comes to you" — this piece is about what comes to us from the dead, from the past. What comes unbidden. I might even subtly echo that. The last line could gesture at it: something about how the dead don't leave us everything, only the parts that come to us—recipes, habits, ways of holding a knife. Hmm, or keep it contained.

Title: "Second Person" — that's a nice title given the thesis about recipes being in the second person. Or "The Imperative Mood." Or "For Whoever Comes Next." Or "Don't Worry If It Cracks." I like "Second Person" as a title—it's clean and pays off in the text.

Let me think about the narrator. First person, a woman probably, but I can leave gender ambiguous or make it a daughter. "Daughter" gives the mother-daughter thread clarity. Let's say the narrator is clearing out the mother's house with her brother, who wants efficiency; she lingers. Small friction: he's already called the dumpster people. She takes the box last, almost as an afterthought.

3. (250 words) Deeper in. The annotations as narrative. Margie. The unknown handwriting. The card in her own child handwriting. The realization about time—the oldest cards from 1961, butter-stained, translucent.
4. (200 words) The meditation: recipes as second-person address. The dead speaking in imperatives. "Don't worry if it cracks."
5. (150 words) The ending: she makes the bread at midnight. The smell. The blank cards. She writes the first line of a new recipe, addressed to the future.

**Second Person**

My brother wanted the house emptied by Friday. He'd rented the dumpster on Monday, and by Wednesday the things our mother had spent sixty years gathering were leaving through the front door in black bags. He was not heartless. He was practical, which can look identical from a distance, and grief had made him more practical still, as though the mess of her possessions were an insult to the clean fact of her death. (71)

I was on a stepstool wiping out the cabinet above the refrigerator when I found the box. Tin, once blue, rusted at the corners. I knew it before I touched it. It had lived up there my whole childhood, brought down only for ceremony—cardamom bread at Christmas, the lamb cake at Easter with its fleece of coconut. (58)

"Taking that?" he asked, not looking up from the shelf he was dismantling.

"It's just recipes," I said. He shrugged. That was the entire negotiation for the heaviest thing I carried out of the house. (16+28=44)

That night I opened it at my own kitchen table, and it was not just recipes. (15)

There were two hundred cards, maybe more. Most in her hand—that quick cursive leaning like something blown sideways. Some in my grandmother's blunt pencil. A few in a looping script I couldn't place, women who had been dead longer than I'd been alive, passing a pie crust down through the tin like a rumor. The printed dividers said BREADS, DESSERTS, MAIN DISHES, but she had added her own tabs in ballpoint: COMPANY. SICK. FOR BAD DAYS. (82)

Under FOR BAD DAYS, a dark chocolate cake with one layer, titled in 1974: Divorce Cake. On the back—Made this the day it was final. Ate half of it standing at the counter. Do not judge me. (36)

Under SICK, a rice pudding. On the back, in different ink, added years later: for fevers. For heartbreak. For Tuesdays. (21)

I sat with the box for three hours. My tea went cold twice. It was like reading a diary that happened to be organized by course. Here was her handwriting young and careful, then quick, then shaky at the end. Here was a lemon square with the note: Margie asked for this at every visit for thirty years and I always said no. She can have it now. I never knew who Margie was. My mother had a Margie—a whole person, a thirty-year campaign of withheld lemon squares—and I never knew. (93)

And then, filed in DESSERTS between the lemon squares and the shortbread, in fat pencil letters: PANCAKS. 1. pour. 2. wate. 3. flip wen bubuls. Mine. I was seven. She had kept it for forty years in the place where she kept the recipes that mattered, as though a seven-year-old's pancakes were part of the canon. (55)

I don't have children. My brother's kids are grown and far away. There is no one to leave this box to, and I sat there understanding that she probably knew that, and kept the cards anyway, and that maybe keeping things no one will inherit is its own kind of hope, or its own kind of letter. (59)

Because here is what I noticed, somewhere around midnight, holding a card for beef stew that still smelled faintly of bay leaves: every recipe is written in the second person. All of them. Cream the butter. Fold in the eggs gently—don't stir; you'll knock the air out. Let it rest. You'll know it's done when you can smell it from the other room. She never used a timer, my mother. She used the house. She used her nose standing in the doorway in her slippers. And every instruction on every card was addressed to a you she could not see and did not name—someone in a kitchen she would never stand in, still alive because she once was. (124)

The dead can't tell us anything, we say. But they can instruct us. Instruction is what they have. Turn the dough once. Don't open the oven door. Don't worry if it cracks. (31)

That last one was on the back of the cheesecake card, in her late, shaking hand, underlined twice: Don't worry if it cracks. It's going to crack. (27)

I made the cardamom bread at one in the morning because I could not not make it. I didn't have enough cardamom, so I substituted, as her own cards taught me: cinnamon and a little black pepper, nobody's grandmother will know. I creamed the butter. I kneaded it the number of times she specified, which was not minutes but turns—forty turns, then stop, you're not mad at it. The house began to smell like every December of my life arriving at once, and I stood in the doorway in my slippers like a woman checking her own nose, and I understood her completely for the first time in thirty years and thirty seconds. (115)

The loaf cracked down the middle. It's going to crack. (10)

It didn't taste like hers. It tasted like mine—near hers, the way my face in certain mirrors is near hers, mine and hers at once. I ate it warm at the counter, standing up, which I believe is the correct way, and which I believe she would have judged me gently for, and then joined me. (56)

At the very back of the tin, under a rubber band, was a fresh pack of blank cards. She'd bought them and never got to them. There was always more time; that's the belief you live inside; that's the whole trick of being alive. (45)

So I took one out and started a card. Cardamom bread, with my corrections, my substitutions, the turns counted my way. And when I got to the part where it goes in the pan, I wrote what she would have written, what all of us are always writing, forward into kitchens we will never see, to a you I can't imagine yet: (63)

You'll know it's ready when the house smells like someone is coming home. (13)
